blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — PPE shortage surge-capacity strategies
stem: Which statement best describes crisis-capacity PPE strategies during a severe shortage?

options.A: Use crisis strategies temporarily during a known shortage when supply cannot meet current utilization, after considering contingency measures.
options.B: Use crisis strategies when future supply is uncertain even though current inventory still meets the facility's present utilization rate.
options.C: Continue crisis strategies after supply again meets utilization so the facility can rebuild inventory before returning to routine practice.
options.D: Move to crisis strategies before contingency when demand rises rapidly because crisis measures conserve the greatest amount of PPE.

rationale: A is correct. CDC/NIOSH defines crisis capacity as temporary strategies for known PPE shortages when supply cannot meet the facility's current utilization rate. Crisis strategies pose the highest risk and should follow consideration of conventional and contingency approaches; facilities should promptly resume conventional practices as PPE availability improves. B describes contingency capacity, in which current supply may still meet utilization but future adequacy is uncertain. C incorrectly continues crisis measures after supply recovers. D reverses the intended sequence by moving to crisis before contingency.
educational_objective: Distinguish crisis-capacity PPE strategies from conventional and contingency approaches: crisis measures are temporary, higher-risk options for known shortages when supply cannot meet current utilization and should end as adequate supply returns.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) / National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH); National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
source_document_title: Conserving Supplies of Personal Protective Equipment in Healthcare Facilities during Shortages; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
source_version_date: CDC/NIOSH page dated October 22, 2024 and rechecked 2026-08-21; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective April 2026
source_locator: CDC/NIOSH Surge capacity: conventional, contingency, and crisis definitions; crisis strategies may be used temporarily during known PPE shortages, pose the highest risk, and may be considered when supply cannot meet current utilization. PPE supply conservation strategies: contingency then crisis augment conventional strategies and are meant to be considered sequentially; promptly resume standard conventional practices as PPE availability increases. NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan printed p.8: apply infection-prevention principles, protect health care personnel, and promote staff/workplace safety.
source_claim_supported: Current CDC/NIOSH guidance directly supports the known-shortage/current-utilization trigger, temporary nature, higher risk, sequential consideration, and return to conventional practice as supply improves.
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control, printed p.8: infection prevention, environmental/workplace safety, and protection of health care personnel.
pdf_visual_verification: PASS — official 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan printed p.8 was screenshot-verified on 2026-08-21 and visibly includes infection-prevention and staff/workplace-safety activity statements.

option_audit.A: Correct; matches CDC/NIOSH crisis-capacity definition and sequencing.
option_audit.B: Plausible shortage-planning scenario but describes contingency capacity rather than crisis capacity.
option_audit.C: Plausible inventory-conservation rationale but conflicts with guidance to resume conventional practice as supply improves.
option_audit.D: Plausible urgency-based escalation but reverses the intended sequential use of contingency before crisis measures.

cueing_audit.answer_length: Final option lengths are balanced: A 142, B 136, C 139, D 131 characters; the key is not uniquely conspicuous.
cueing_audit.absolute_words: No distractor depends on a simplistic always/never/only cue.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: No defensible second answer identified: B is contingency capacity, C continues crisis measures after recovery, and D reverses the recommended sequence.
